issues.issue: The execution date is left as "July KX, 2005", i.e. a blank/garbled day, which matters because the Restricted Period in Definitions D runs three years from "the date of this Agreement". The missing day is a mechanical defect that could require construction of when the covenant expires.

The first sentence is an incomplete sentence (a "Pursuant to..." clause with no predicate), and the recital's list of Sellers is punctuated so that the Buyer/Sellers grouping is grammatically detached from the purchase sentence. The error is presentational and does not obviously change any obligation.

This recital imports undefined capitalized terms from the Stock Purchase Agreement, but the entire-agreement clause in Miscellaneous A says this Agreement supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements on its subject matter, leaving the status of the imported definitions (e.g. "Acquired Companies" used in Definitions C) open. A court could be asked whether the SPA definitions still control.

The long enumerated list of services ends with the qualifier "of health insurance claims for hospitals and physicians in the United States", and it is genuinely unclear whether that qualifier (and its geographic limit) attaches to every listed service or only to the closing data-conversion items. The reach of "consulting", "audits" and "call center services", and whether services performed offshore for U.S. providers are within "the Business", are open to two readings.

The definition is circular and self-referential: "Company" is defined to include any entity that is a "successor, subsidiary or affiliate of the Company", using the term inside its own definition, and it names "Ajuba" which is nowhere defined. The boundary of the protected entity group is therefore uncertain.

This expanded definition conflicts with the preamble, which defines "the Company" as Ajuba International, Inc. alone, so the same defined term carries two different scopes across the instrument. Which meaning governs the covenants in Section 2 and the assignment carve-out in Successors and Assigns is contestable.

The definition turns on the undefined imported term "Acquired Companies" and on vague qualifiers — "actively sought" as a prospective client and "material contact" — with the further ambiguity that the "material contact" limitation grammatically attaches only to subclause (c). Whether limbs (a) and (b), which have no contact or currency limit for Buyer clients, sweep in customers the Shareholder never dealt with is open to argument.

"The United States, its territories and protectorates" is territorially precise on its face, but read with Section 2.A.1's phrase "directly or indirectly in the Restricted Area engage in any activity" it does not say whether work performed abroad for United States customers is inside or outside the Area. That situs question is the kind a court must resolve.

"Directly or indirectly in the Restricted Area engage in any activity which is in competition with the Business" is both vague as to what counts as competing activity and ambiguous as to whether "in the Restricted Area" modifies the place of the activity or the place of the competition. The list of capacities also closes with the catch-all "or otherwise", raising an ejusdem generis question about its reach.

The clause both acknowledges the restrictions are "reasonable in scope and duration" and instructs a court to reform them if adjudged unenforceable, an internal tension a court must resolve when applying its own reasonableness test. The reformation direction is otherwise conventional and self-contained.
